chapter_theme: These sixteen closing verses mostly grade conduct and learning: five marks of the good giver and the lay vows set above scripture, the trick of the calf-skin placed beside killing, two tiers of the learned, five dogs answered by five easy virtues, a ladder from sweet speech to release, virtues fitted to the station where they cost most, and a ranking that puts Ganga worship below restraint, ending with worth proved only at death.

81.reading: The verse names five marks of a man (he does not grieve over what has passed, does not crave what is out of his hand, takes no pleasure in base things, speaks softly, and gives what the poor ask with a heart that melts) and says such a man is praised by the gods in sweet words.
81.nuance: The last two marks belong together: the soft word and the melting heart are the manner of the gift, so the list ends in giving done well, not giving alone. கைலாரா is hard to construe; read here as what has not come into the hand.

items.claim: one who does not grieve over what has passed is praised by the gods
one who does not crave what is not in his hand is praised
one who takes no delight in base things is praised
one who answers the poor in soft words is praised
one who gives with a heart that melts within is praised

82.reading: The verse names five marks of a man (he sees his house, lovely to the eye, as a wilderness, others' wealth as a potsherd, others' wives as the mother who bore him, he does not go between people stringing harsh words, and he does not kill) and asks what he would lack even without the recitation of the many scriptures.
82.nuance: The five line up with the Jain lay vows: non-attachment, not stealing, not desiring another's wife, no slander or untruth, not killing. The closing question sets this conduct above scriptural recitation; பல்லவர் ஒத்தினால் is read as ஓத்து, scripture, which the spelling leaves open.

items.claim: a house sweet to the eye is to be seen as a wilderness
others' wealth is to be seen as a potsherd
another's wife is to be seen as one's own mother
one does not go between people stringing harsh words together
one does not kill

83.reading: The verse says that those on the side of virtue do not milk a cow by showing it a stuffed calf-skin, do not drink milk so drawn, do not do what brings blame and sin, and do not seize creatures living content in what they have, ruining their homes to Death's delight.
83.nuance: The first two items are one practice seen from milker and drinker: the deceit worked on the cow whose calf is dead taints the milk too. The list runs from that small cruelty to the killing of creatures, so the trick on the cow is placed on the same line as killing. The construal of கறந்தபால் with பாற்பட்டார் is a reading.

items.claim: the good do not milk a cow by showing it a calf's skin
the good do not drink milk drawn that way
the good do not do what brings blame
the good do not do what brings sin
the good do not seize contented creatures and destroy their homes for Death's pleasure

84.reading: The verse names five things not wanted where elders are seated (laughter, private counsel, partiality to friends, enmity, and song or idle talk) and says the ancient treatises set this down after those who knew had examined it.
84.nuance: It cites old treatises as its authority, an appeal the verses around it rarely make. நட்டார்க்கு வாரம் is read as favouring one's friends, a fault of judgment in an assembly rather than of manners.

items.claim: laughter is not wanted where elders sit
private consultation is not wanted where elders sit
partiality to friends is not wanted where elders sit
enmity is not wanted where elders sit
song or idle talk is not wanted where elders sit

85.reading: The verse names five branches of knowledge (grammar of sound, true knowledge, logic, the religious systems, and release as the wise have seen it) and says one who knows all five is, on reflection, a learned man of the first rank.
85.nuance: சத்தமெய்ஞ் ஞானம் is divided as சத்தம் and மெய்ஞ்ஞானம். The verse ranks learning, and ranks it by subject: release closes the list as the highest thing to be known. It is the first of a pair; verse 86 names the middle rank.

items.claim: knowing the science of sound and grammar marks the first-rank learned man
knowing true knowledge marks him
knowing logic marks him
knowing the religious systems marks him
knowing release as the wise have seen it marks him

86.reading: The verse names five arts (one read as the art of the eye, arithmetic, the lute, the making of unguents, and cutting and arranging leaves) and says one who knows these five is reckoned a learned man of the middle rank.
86.nuance: Set against verse 85, the pair grades learning: doctrine and release make the first rank, crafts and accomplishments the middle. The first item, கண்ணும், is unclear; it may name an art of the eye such as painting or the reading of signs, or be only 'also'.

items.claim: an art of the eye, if that is the sense, marks the middle-rank learned man
arithmetic marks him
the lute marks him
the making of unguents marks him
cutting and arranging leaves marks him

87.reading: The verse names five men who are dogs: the shameless, the one who does not befriend well, the one who does not honour the great, the one in another's service, and the one with nothing in his hand who goes to the quarter of the jewelled courtesans.
87.nuance: பருத்தி பகர்வழி, the lane where cotton is sold, is hard to fit; it may mark where the penniless man loiters or compare him to a dog in that lane. பிறர் சேவகன் may mean a servant or a soldier of another man. Verse 88 answers this list item by item.

items.claim: the shameless man is a dog
one who does not form good friendships is a dog
one who does not honour the great is a dog
one who is another's servant is a dog
one with nothing in hand who goes to the courtesans' quarter is a dog

88.reading: The verse says, to a woman addressed, that modesty comes easily to womanhood, laughter to a friend, steadfastness to a soldier, and reverence to the great, while arrows seldom fly at a man of compassion.
88.nuance: It reverses verse 87 point by point: shame, friendship, the சேவகன் and honour of the great return, now as what comes easily. The last item turns from easy to rare, which is the list's twist. ஏண் is read as steadfastness and அளியன் as the compassionate man; both are readings.

items.claim: modesty is easy to womanhood
laughter is easy if one is a friend
steadfastness is easy if one is a soldier
reverence is easy toward the great
for an arrow to fly at a compassionate man is rare

norm.note: a period claim about women: modesty treated as natural to womanhood

89.reading: The verse traces a chain: sweet speech makes kin, harsh speech without good nature makes enemies, gentle speech brings unceasing grace, and that grace, in a good mind, becomes release that does not perish.
89.nuance: The things are steps, not peers: speech leads to grace, grace to release, so the list is a ladder from manners to salvation; the Tamil gives four steps, not five.

items.claim: sweet speech produces kinship
harsh speech without good nature produces enmity
gentle speech produces unceasing grace
grace in a good mind becomes undying release

90.reading: The verse says penance befits a young man, refusing food befits a rich man, and beauty befits a chaste woman, but a man with shoulders strong and fair who lacks understanding becomes like a red ant in the shade.
90.nuance: Each virtue is fitting where it costs most: penance while youth pulls the other way, fasting when food is at hand. The fourth item turns from fitting to unfitting. தழல் may belong with a third தக்கது, and the image of the ant in the shade is read as a nuisance where one rests; the count of four is the Tamil's, not the title's five.

items.claim: penance is fitting in a young man
refusing food is fitting in a rich man
beauty is fitting in a chaste woman
a strong-shouldered man without understanding is like a red ant in the shade

norm.note: a period norm: a woman's beauty counted fitting only with chastity

91.reading: The verse sets out claims that heaven comes by falsehood and hell by truth, and that wealth and a dark-eyed maiden make life sweet, and tells the woman addressed that if this were true, it would be no harm to take up any penance at all.
91.nuance: Read as a reductio: the inverted claims about heaven and hell are absurd, so the conclusion drawn from them is mocked. The spacing of line 1 (வா யால்நிர யம்) and the sense of the close are unsure, and the verse may be read otherwise. It gives four claims, not five, divided at each instrument (falsehood, truth, wealth, the maiden).

items.claim: heaven is said to come by falsehood
hell is said to come by truth
wealth is said to make life sweet
a dark-eyed maiden is said to make life sweet

92.reading: The verse says household life is better than a mean dharma and worth guarding, since one can walk with the truly virtuous, and that those who cooked, served and then ate, feeding the virtuous, will live in this life too cooking, serving and eating in plenty.
92.nuance: It does not set household above renunciation as such, only above புல்லறம், a poor or false dharma. The repeated அட்டிட்டுண்டு makes the reward the same act again: feeding now brings the means to feed later. The verse argues rather than counts; the three items are its three claims.

items.claim: household life is better than a mean dharma
in it one can walk with the virtuous
those who cooked, served and ate will live so again

93.reading: The verse says giving is good and withholding evil, joining the good is good and joining those who are not is evil, and that one who keeps hearing and stands firm has a penance that carries him, riding, to the flawless high state.
93.nuance: The first four items are two pairs of good and evil; the fifth is an instruction whose fruit is the high state. Hearing and holding firm are themselves called a penance.

items.claim: giving is good
not giving is evil
joining the good is good
joining those who are not good is evil
hearing without ceasing and standing firm is a penance that leads to the high state

94.reading: The verse ranks conduct: not going where others are eating, where enemies are brought low, or where counsel is taken, is foremost; ending quarrels of words after reflection is high penance; and, beside these, the worship on the bank of the Ganga is lowest.
94.nuance: The three ranks (தலை, உயர், கடை) put restraint first and pilgrimage worship last, so a celebrated rite is counted but placed beneath manners of speech and presence. உரைப்பூசல் கோறல் may instead mean wordy quarrels and killing; கோறல் usually means killing.

items.claim: not going where others eat is foremost
not going where enemies are brought low is foremost
not going where counsel is taken is foremost
ending quarrels of words is high penance
worship on the Ganga's bank is lowest

95.reading: The verse names five (the chaste wife, the soldier, the flawless ascetic of severe penance, the man upright in dealings with wealth, and the worthy who keep a trust without flaw and judge cases) and says their rightness should be known when they have died.
95.nuance: The test is deferred to death: none of these virtues can be certified while the life can still fail. The list spans house, war, renunciation, trade and judgment, so the claim covers every station.

items.claim: the chaste wife's rightness is known after death
the soldier's rightness is known after death
the flawless ascetic's rightness is known after death
the man upright in wealth's dealings is known after death
the worthy who keep a trust and judge are known after death

96.reading: The verse names conduct it calls aram (following the right path, not grieving, truthfulness, attending to intent, and turning in disgust from words joined with evil speech) and says the learned who would be saved examine and let the rest go.
96.nuance: Several words are unclear: வாயல் may be a misprint, and வழிப்படரல் and குறிப்படரல் could mean pursuing a path or a sign in either a good or bad sense. The division into five is a reading.

items.claim: following the right path is aram
not grieving is aram
truthfulness is aram
attending to intent is aram
turning in disgust from words joined with evil speech is aram

links.note: Kural 92 ranks a glad face and sweet speech above giving with a glad heart; the verse joins soft words and a melting gift in one man.
links.teaches: The Kural separates sweet speech from giving and ranks speech higher; the verse refuses the choice and makes the soft word the manner in which the gift is given.
links.list_adds: It places soft speech and the melting gift side by side as the last two of five marks, after inner restraints, so speech and gift become one closing act rather than rivals.

links.note: Kural 134 says forgotten Veda can be relearnt but a brahmin's birth is ruined if conduct fails; the verse asks what a man of five vows lacks without the scriptures.
links.teaches: Both rank conduct above scriptural recitation, but the Kural keeps the brahmin and his birth in view while the verse makes the point for any man who keeps five lay vows.
links.list_adds: It names what the conduct is (five vows against attachment, theft, adultery, slander and killing) where the couplet speaks only of conduct in general.

links.note: Verse 18 promises no further birth to one who does not lie, steal, desire women or eat flesh; verse 82 lists nearly the same vows and sets them above scripture.
links.teaches: Read together, the same vows earn two fruits in this book: release from rebirth in one verse, and freedom from needing the scriptures in the other.

links.note: Naladiyar 279 makes a cow milked by force the image of the base giver; the verse names milking by a stuffed calf-skin as a cruelty the good refuse.
links.teaches: The quatrain uses forced milking only as a figure for grudging gifts; the verse shows the literal act was itself judged wrong, so the image carried moral weight before it became a figure.
links.list_adds: It sets the milking trick in a list that ends with killing creatures, so a small deceit on an animal is ranked with taking life, which the quatrain's figure never claims.

links.note: Kural 694 says to suppress whispers and shared smiles before the great; the verse lists five things not wanted where elders sit.
links.teaches: The couplet's two signs are about what a ruler might read into them; the verse widens the rule to elders generally and adds faults of judgment such as favouring friends.
links.list_adds: It adds counsel, partiality to friends, enmity and song to the couplet's laughter, and cites the old treatises as its authority, turning a courtier's caution into a code of the assembly.

links.note: Verse 85 names five subjects that make a first-rank learned man; verse 86 names five arts that make a middle-rank one.
links.teaches: Together they grade learning in tiers: doctrine, logic and release make the first rank, while arithmetic, music and crafts make only the middle.

links.note: Verse 87 calls five men dogs for lacking shame, friendship and reverence or for serving another; verse 88 names shame, friendship, the soldier and reverence as what comes easily.
links.teaches: The second verse answers the first word for word, so the pair shows the same qualities as failures in one man and as natural ease in their proper holders.

links.note: Kural 98 says sweet speech free of pettiness brings joy here and hereafter; the verse runs sweet speech through kinship and grace to release.
links.teaches: The Kural promises joy in two worlds; the verse names the mechanism, speech producing grace and grace producing release, and sets harsh speech's enmity beside it.
links.list_adds: Its items are links in a chain rather than peers, so the list becomes a ladder from manners to release, a sequence the couplet does not draw.

links.note: Kural 160 grants greatness to those who fast but ranks them after those who bear harsh words; the verse says refusing food befits a rich man.
links.teaches: The Kural ranks fasting as a whole; the verse makes its worth depend on who fasts, fitting most where food is plentiful and the refusal costs something.
links.list_adds: It pairs each virtue with the person in whom it costs most (penance with youth, fasting with wealth, beauty with chastity), a matching of virtue to station the couplet lacks.

links.note: Kural 46 asks what one gains by leaving a virtuous household for the outside way; the verse says household life is better than a mean dharma.
links.teaches: The Kural's question reaches toward renunciation itself; the verse limits the claim to a poor or false dharma, a narrower comparison from a Jain text that honours the ascetic.
links.list_adds: It adds the fruit of the household, that feeding the virtuous returns as the means to feed again, which the couplet's rhetorical question does not name.

links.note: Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world; the verse sets giving with good company and steady hearing and promises the high state.
links.teaches: The Kural cuts giving loose from reward by a hypothetical; the verse binds it back to a destination, showing the two works disagree on whether the fruit is part of the reason.
links.list_adds: It pairs giving and company each with its opposite and caps them with hearing as a penance, so giving becomes one step on a road to the high state.

links.note: The Siddhar verse asks what use ash and bathing are without learning to be born otherwise; the verse ranks worship on the Ganga's bank lowest, below restraint.
links.teaches: The Siddhar dismisses ritual bathing outright, while the ethics verse keeps Ganga worship as a merit but ranks it beneath restraint of presence and speech.
links.list_adds: Its ranking into foremost, high and lowest places the rite in an order of merits rather than rejecting it.

links.note: Kural 114 says the worthy and unworthy are seen by what each leaves behind; the verse says the rightness of five kinds of person is known when they die.
links.teaches: Both defer judgment of worth past the life; the verse applies the rule to five stations and names death as the moment of proof.
links.list_adds: It runs the test through wife, soldier, ascetic, trader and arbiter, so one rule of posthumous judgment is made to cover every station of life.

source_issues: 83 and 89: the site's text lacks line 1 (text flag site_diff), so those lines rest on one source.
81 line 1: கைலாரா is hard to construe.
86 line 1: கண்ணும் is unclear as the first of the five arts.
87 line 4: பருத்தி பகர்வழி does not fit the list clearly.
91 line 1: the spacing வா யால்நிர யம் looks broken (வாயால் நிரயம்).
96 line 1: வாயல் is unclear and may be a misprint; line 2 தீக்சொற்க is probably a misprint for தீச்சொற்க.
